events/pentecost-30/summary: According to Acts 2, some fifty days after Jesus' crucifixion his followers gathered in Jerusalem experienced the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, spoke in other tongues and Peter preached to pilgrims from across the diaspora. Christians of every tradition treat the day as the birth of the Church, and the existence of a Jerusalem community led by Peter, John and James is historically secure.
events/pentecost-30/causes/1: Jewish pilgrimage festival of Shavuot gathered diaspora Jews in Jerusalem
events/pentecost-30/consequences/0: Formation of the first Christian community in Jerusalem
events/pentecost-30/consequences/1: Pattern of Spirit-baptism later central to Pentecostal theology
events/pentecost-30/consequences/2: Mission to the diaspora implied by the list of nations in Acts 2
events/ethiopian-official-baptized-34/ti: Philip baptizes an Ethiopian court official
events/ethiopian-official-baptized-34/su: Acts 8 tells how Philip the evangelist baptized a eunuch, treasurer of the Kandake (queen) of 'Ethiopia' — the Nubian kingdom of Meroë — on the road to Gaza. Ethiopian Christians regard the story as the first seed of the faith in Africa beyond Egypt, though no organised church is attested in the region until the fourth century.
events/ethiopian-official-baptized-34/ca: Dispersal of Hellenist believers after the death of Stephen
events/ethiopian-official-baptized-34/co: Symbol of African Christianity's apostolic roots
Frequently cited in Ethiopian Orthodox self-understanding
events/conversion-of-paul-34/title: Conversion of Paul on the Damascus road
events/conversion-of-paul-34/summary: Saul of Tarsus, a Pharisee who had persecuted the followers of Jesus, experienced a vision of the risen Christ near Damascus (Galatians 1; Acts 9, 22, 26). He became the most influential missionary and theologian of the first generation, insisting that Gentiles be received without circumcision.
events/conversion-of-paul-34/causes/0: Paul's zeal against the early Jesus movement
events/conversion-of-paul-34/consequence: Pauline letters, the earliest Christian writings
events/christians-named-at-antioch-40/su: Acts 11:26 records that at Antioch, the third city of the Roman Empire, Jews and Gentiles worshipped together and the disciples were first called Christianoi. Antioch became the base of the Gentile mission and later one of the great patriarchates.
events/christians-named-at-antioch-40/ca: Hellenist believers preached to Greeks after Stephen's martyrdom
events/christians-named-at-antioch-40/co: Antioch becomes the launch-point for Paul and Barnabas
Christian identity distinct from other Jewish groups begins to form
events/pauls-first-journey-46/title: Paul and Barnabas's first missionary journey
events/pauls-first-journey-46/summary: Sent out by the church of Antioch, Paul and Barnabas preached in Cyprus and the cities of southern Galatia (Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, Derbe). Their reception of uncircumcised Gentile converts raised the question settled at the Jerusalem council.
events/council-of-jerusalem-49/summary: Apostles and elders met in Jerusalem to decide whether Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses. Led by James, with Peter and Paul testifying, they ruled that Gentiles need only abstain from idolatry, blood, strangled meat and sexual immorality (Acts 15; compare Galatians 2).
events/council-of-jerusalem-49/longText: Often called the first church council, the Jerusalem meeting addressed the most explosive question of the first generation: was faith in Jesus a form of Judaism that Gentiles must enter through circumcision, or did the Messiah open a new people of God in which Jew and Gentile stood on equal footing? Acts presents Peter recounting the conversion of Cornelius, Paul and Barnabas reporting signs among the Gentiles, and James citing Amos before issuing a decree with four minimal requirements. Paul's own account in Galatians 2 emphasises a private agreement dividing mission fields, and the later incident at Antioch shows that table fellowship remained contested. Catholic and Orthodox writers see in the meeting a model of conciliar authority; Protestants stress its appeal to Scripture and the grace of God. Historians debate how Acts 15 and Galatians 2 relate, but agree that the outcome made a law-free Gentile mission possible.
events/council-of-jerusalem-49/causes/0: Gentile conversions in Antioch and Galatia
events/council-of-jerusalem-49/causes/1: Pressure from Judean believers who required circumcision
events/council-of-jerusalem-49/consequen: Gradual parting of the ways between church and synagogue
events/earliest-pauline-letter-50/title: Paul writes 1 Thessalonians, the earliest Christian text
events/earliest-pauline-letter-50/summar: During his eighteen-month stay at Corinth, Paul wrote to the young church at Thessalonica — most likely the oldest surviving Christian document. His letters to Galatians, Corinthians and Romans over the following decade set the agenda for Christian theology on grace, the Law, the church and resurrection.
events/earliest-pauline-letter-50/causes: Paul's second journey into Macedonia and Achaia
events/earliest-pauline-letter-50/conseq: Foundational texts for later debates on justification
events/thomas-in-india-52/summary: The St Thomas Christians of Kerala hold that the apostle Thomas landed at Muziris in AD 52, founded seven churches and was martyred at Mylapore near Chennai around 72. The Acts of Thomas (3rd century) link him to India; Roman trade with the Malabar coast makes an early mission plausible, though firm evidence of Indian Christians dates from later centuries.
events/thomas-in-india-52/causes/0: Roman–Indian spice trade through the Red Sea
events/thomas-in-india-52/consequences/0: Identity of the Thomas Christians (Syro-Malabar, Malankara and others)
events/thomas-in-india-52/consequences/1: Later ties with the Church of the East
events/mark-in-alexandria-60/title: Mark founds the church of Alexandria (tradition)
events/mark-in-alexandria-60/summary: Eusebius records the tradition that Mark the evangelist was the first to preach in Egypt and founded the church in Alexandria. The Coptic Orthodox Church counts its popes in unbroken succession from Mark, whom it honours as martyr; reliable records of Alexandrian Christianity begin in the second century.
events/mark-in-alexandria-60/consequence: Alexandria becomes a leading see and intellectual centre
Coptic identity as 'the See of St Mark'
events/addai-mission-to-edessa-60/summar: Syriac tradition, preserved by Eusebius and the Doctrine of Addai, says that King Abgar of Edessa corresponded with Jesus and was healed by Addai (Thaddaeus), one of the Seventy. The legend is not historical in its details, but Edessa became the cradle of Syriac-speaking Christianity by the late second century.
events/addai-mission-to-edessa-60/causes: Edessa's position on trade routes between Rome and Parthia
events/addai-mission-to-edessa-60/conseq: Edessa's self-image as the first Christian city
Foundational legend for Syriac churches east and west
events/martyrdom-of-james-62/title: Martyrdom of James, brother of the Lord
events/martyrdom-of-james-62/summary: Josephus reports that the high priest Ananus had James 'the brother of Jesus who was called Christ' stoned during an interregnum between Roman governors. James had led the Jerusalem church and embodied a Torah-observant Jewish Christianity.
events/martyrdom-of-james-62/causes/0: Tension between the priestly aristocracy and the Jerusalem church
events/martyrdom-of-james-62/consequence: Leadership of the Jerusalem church passes to Symeon
Weakening of Jewish-Christian leadership before the war
events/neronian-persecution-64/summary: After the great fire of Rome in July 64, Nero blamed the Christians; Tacitus describes victims torn by dogs, crucified and burned as torches. Strong early tradition holds that Peter and Paul were executed in Rome in this period.
events/neronian-persecution-64/consequen: Martyrdom tradition of Peter and Paul at Rome
Christianity identified by Roman authorities as distinct from Judaism
events/fall-of-jerusalem-70/title: Fall of Jerusalem and destruction of the Temple
events/fall-of-jerusalem-70/summary: Roman legions under Titus captured Jerusalem and destroyed the Second Temple, ending the Jewish revolt begun in 66. Eusebius reports that the Jerusalem Christians had fled to Pella. The catastrophe reshaped both rabbinic Judaism and Christianity and accelerated their separation.
events/fall-of-jerusalem-70/consequences: Decline of Jerusalem as Christian centre
Christian interpretation of the fall as fulfilment of Jesus' warnings (Mark 13)
events/revelation-on-patmos-95/summary: The Book of Revelation, addressed to seven churches of Asia, was written by a prophet named John exiled on Patmos, most likely under Domitian. Its visions of the Lamb, the beast and the New Jerusalem have shaped Christian worship, art and eschatology ever since; authorship and dating are debated.
events/revelation-on-patmos-95/causes/0: Pressure of the imperial cult in Asia Minor
events/revelation-on-patmos-95/consequen: Canonical status long disputed in the East
events/first-clement-96/title: Clement of Rome writes to Corinth
events/first-clement-96/summary: The church of Rome, through Clement, wrote to the Corinthian church urging reinstatement of deposed presbyters and grounding church order in apostolic succession. 1 Clement is the earliest Christian writing outside the New Testament and an important witness to early church office.
events/first-clement-96/causes/0: Factional dispute in the Corinthian church
events/first-clement-96/consequences/1: Evidence of Roman concern for other churches
events/ignatius-letters-110/title: Ignatius of Antioch writes on the road to martyrdom
events/ignatius-letters-110/summary: Bishop Ignatius of Antioch, taken under guard to Rome to die in the arena, wrote seven letters to churches in Asia Minor and Rome. They urge unity around the bishop, presbyters and deacons, insist on the real humanity of Christ against docetists, and call the Eucharist 'the medicine of immortality'.
events/ignatius-letters-110/consequences: Earliest witness to the single bishop (monepiscopate)
events/pliny-trajan-letters-112/title: Pliny's letter to Trajan on the Christians
events/pliny-trajan-letters-112/summary: As governor of Bithynia-Pontus, Pliny the Younger asked Trajan how to treat Christians, describing their dawn meetings to sing a hymn 'to Christ as to a god' and their shared meal. Trajan replied that they were not to be hunted out, but if accused and obstinate they should be punished.
events/pliny-trajan-letters-112/causes/0: Christianity spreading in town and countryside
events/pliny-trajan-letters-112/conseque: Legal pattern of sporadic, accusation-driven persecution for over a century
events/bar-kokhba-revolt-132/title: Bar Kokhba revolt and Aelia Capitolina
events/bar-kokhba-revolt-132/summary: The second Jewish revolt under Simon bar Kokhba was crushed by Hadrian, who refounded Jerusalem as the pagan colony Aelia Capitolina and banned Jews from the city. Jewish Christians who would not accept Bar Kokhba as messiah suffered from both sides, and the Jerusalem church thereafter had Gentile bishops.
events/bar-kokhba-revolt-132/consequence: Deepening separation of church and synagogue
events/marcion-excommunicated-144/title: Marcion breaks with the Roman church
events/marcion-excommunicated-144/summar: Marcion, a wealthy shipowner from Sinope, taught that the God of the Old Testament was a lesser, just deity distinct from the loving Father revealed by Jesus. Expelled by the Roman church, he organised a rival church with a canon of an edited Luke and ten Pauline letters.
events/marcion-excommunicated-144/causes: Pauline contrast of Law and gospel pushed to an extreme
events/marcion-excommunicated-144/conseq: Marcionite churches across the empire into the 5th century
Stimulus to defining the New Testament canon and affirming the Old Testament
events/justin-first-apology-155/summary: Justin, a convert philosopher teaching in Rome, addressed Antoninus Pius defending Christians against charges of atheism and immorality. His Apology presents Christ as the Logos who seeded truth in philosophers and gives the earliest detailed description of Sunday Eucharist and baptism. He was martyred around 165.
events/justin-first-apology-155/causes/0: Pagan slanders and legal vulnerability of Christians
events/justin-first-apology-155/conseque: Model of Christian engagement with philosophy
events/martyrdom-of-polycarp-155/summary: The aged bishop Polycarp of Smyrna, a link to the apostle John, was burned in the stadium after refusing to swear by Caesar's genius: 'Eighty and six years have I served him'. The Martyrdom of Polycarp is the earliest martyr-acts and the first evidence for an annual commemoration at a martyr's tomb.
events/martyrdom-of-polycarp-155/causes/: Refusal to offer the imperial oath
events/martyrdom-of-polycarp-155/consequ: Beginning of the cult of martyrs and their relics
